body_markdown:
There’s no shortage of hand-wringing these days about which jobs artificial intelligence will eliminate next. The list gets longer every month.


Tom Cotter, the host of the Hagerty *Barn Find Hunter* video series, has a different kind of answer. While touring Mike Nickels’[woody restoration shop](https://youtu.be/fiJlHh4pfxI?si=lVqFTLIw9e9CKciF) outside Traverse City, Michigan, Cotter stopped mid-sentence and did something unusual—he made a pitch directly to the camera. “If you have time on your hands, want to learn a trade, and want to secure a job that AI can never do,” he said, “get in touch with Hagerty and we’ll connect you with Mike.”


Jordan Lewis


Nickels spent more than 40 years restoring wood-bodied cars before losing his entire shop in a[massive fire in September 2021](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/even-after-a-fire-destroyed-his-michigan-workshop-this-renowned-woody-wagon-restorer-isnt-quitting/) . The small world of woody enthusiasts feared one of the few remaining craftsmen capable of restoring their cars might decide the fire was the right excuse to pack it in. The tenacious and passionate Nickels rebuilt, however, and is back in business. Cotter, who profiled Nickels for the *Barn Find Hunter* back in 2019, returned for a check-in.


Jordan Lewis


Jordan Lewis


Jordan Lewis


In the video, Cotter delves into the art and challenges of crafting wooden bodies. It’s a fiddly business that requires intimate knowledge of specific woods, where to source them, and how to position the grain structure for the proper look. He and Nickels also debate what sort of demand remains for the wooden cars that were popular a century ago.


By the fifties, automakers began replacing real wooden car bodies with metal ones that were wallpapered with fake wood decals. That style continued for decades on cars like the Chrysler Town & Country and the Jeep Grand Wagoneer. But if we’ve learned anything about truly old cars, it’s that there’s always someone with an interest. Ford Model Ts certainly have not disappeared, and Hagerty’s own rally master, Dave Hord, recently chronicled his trip across the Canadian Rockies[in a Ford Model A](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/driving-canadas-most-challenging-roads-in-a-100-year-old-ford/) .


Andrew Holliday


Niche vehicles survive when enough people decide they’re worth keeping alive—and by most accounts, the supply of woody cars remains healthy, and there are plenty of people interested in owning and preserving them. Which brings us back to Cotter’s impromptu camera pitch—and a question worth sitting with.


Who learns this stuff next?


Woody restoration isn’t a job you find on a website. And while McPherson College, a school in Kansas that specializes in automotive restoration, offers a class that focuses on the art of reviving a wood-bodied vehicle, it’s not exactly a certification offered by community colleges across the country. You learn it the way Nickels learned it—starting young, working alongside someone who already knows, absorbing decades of judgment about grain structure and joinery and which corners you cannot cut. It is, as Cotter put it standing in Nickels’ shop, fine cabinetmaking on wheels.


Jordan Lewis


Jordan Lewis


Jordan Lewis


Jordan Lewis


That kind of knowledge transfers one person at a time. And right now, the people who have it are aging out faster than replacements are coming in. Nickels himself joked that what he needs are two 40-year-olds or four 20-year-olds. The laugh was real. So was the math.


In my own automotive pursuits, I frequently come across the same situation: an old-timer performing a specialized skill without a succession plan. There are some exceptions. When my colleague Aaron Robinson and I visited Mike Pierce, who has[refurbished Weber carburetors for decades](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/meet-mike-pierce-the-weber-whisperer/) , we found his grandson working alongside him. Hopefully the kid picks up the torch.


James Lipman


I wonder what the hurdle is. My car buddies see veteran craftsmen with essentially foolproof businesses where demand often outstrips supply. When we hear so much talk about AI replacement, why aren’t members of the Millennial and Gen Z generations banging on their doors hoping to take over?


I’m guessing there are two obstacles: One, many small shops start with a passion. I’ve recently dived into the world of standalone engine computers and found a vibrant community of tuning shops and online forums. There aren’t many graybeards in those shops. The kids dig electronics, not wood-bodied cars.


Secondly, we don’t have a robust apprenticeship culture. I once had a roommate who worked as an engineer at a large automotive company. When the company did a round of layoffs, he lamented that they were foolishly letting all the people who actually knew things walk out the door. When experience and knowledge aren’t coveted, why would those who have it take an interest in passing it along? Without that ingrained culture, the owners of niche shops are probably too busy running their businesses to think about succession. I’ve heard plenty of grumbling that kids just don’t want to work, but based on my experience with many driven twenty-somethings, I flatly reject that.


These are all personal theories, to be sure, but I might be onto something: A few months ago, Ford revealed that, after the company[rehired 350 veteran engineers](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/ford-rehires-veteran-engineers-ai-144332497.html?guccounter=1&guce_referrer=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbS8&guce_referrer_sig=AQAAAFKRDOYSkEJsZXLR99PreCRsJcp7jgrKX84rnDu8B5R3iQEU8p1cDZHF-6cx9dAyVsmBBEZgzqd0iMdECDsquWoRoBrqVi8-cFMWP65TZjrD4oudDbgvRA1ZYilzJE8Dsy5yOr6jZR0s2ivkkcfIg771R00TxL-hoSgZh62EXv3-) , its quality scores jumped. Maybe the tide is shifting. I hope so.


Jordan Lewis


If you know someone running a small niche business, do what Cotter did — encourage others to take up the baton. We need these people to train their successors.
